A short story by this author follows the title characters as they slowly assume the lives of the Stones, who are on vacation, before Bill and Arlene accidentally lock themselves out of their apartment. That story, "Neighbors", is found in a collection along with the stories "Are You A Doctor" and "Bicycles, Muscles, Cigarettes"; that collection is Will You Please Be Quiet, Please? His other works include two stories, one an expansion on the first, about a car accident that kills a boy and the baker who calls about that boy's birthday cake in "The Bath" and "A Small Good Thing". Writing about the death of Anton Chekov in "The Errand" and about Mel, Terri, Laura and Nick discussing the titular concept in another story, what twentieth century American short story writer, the author of "What We Talk About When We Talk About Love"?

In one of his short stories, Ramón Gris is shot by the Nationalists and Pablo Ibbieta's life is saved. It appears in a collection by the same title that contains the stories "The Room," "Erostratus," "Intimacy," and "The Childhood of a Leader," called The Wall. Another of his works takes place in Illyria, where Louis sends a young communist to kill fellow party leader Hoederer. The hitman Hugo does it after seeing Hoederer kissing his wife Jessica, and is later killed by the party. In addition to Dirty Hands, he write about the friend of Ogier P. Who has a relationship with Francoise while clinging to his former lover Anny. That man, Antoine Roquentin, falls victim to the title disease and nearly goes insane in this author's novel Nausea. More famous for a play about a baby-killer, a lesbian murderer, and an army deserter that declares "Hell is other people," name this author of No Exit.

James Wood argued in his essay about this man's "Complacent God" that his writing was more style than content. He has written about a New Jersey teenager who attempted to bomb the Lincoln Tunnel, and published a poetry collection called "Endpoint" and essays called "Due Considerations." In one story, he writes that Stokesie has "two babies chalked up on his fuselage already," and the main character lusts after Queenie, an unknown girl in a bathing suit. Most of his novels are set in fictional Olinger, Pennsylvania and Eastwick, Rhode Island, and they including the Bech books, Buchanan stories, and "The Scarlet Letter" trilogy, while he is best known for a trilogy involving one character, whose first book ends with the pregnancy of his mistress after his legitimate daughter is accidentally drowned. Name this American author of Terrorist and "A&P" best known for his character Harry "Rabbit" Angstrom.

One character in this work gets a relative who pursues her killed, and forces one of her husband's concubines into suicide. Most of this story takes place in the "Grand View" or "Prospect" Garden in the titular place. Wang Xifeng controls the central household by simultaneously charming its matriarch, her grandmother, and using an iron fist with regards to the money. The story chronicles protagonist's frustrations with the bureaucrats he encounters and his compassion for women, whom he views to be superior to men. Throughout the story, Jia Baoyu is destined to marry Xue Baochai, one of his first cousins, instead of his fragile cousin Lin Daiyu. Name this classic of Chinese literature, an 18th century work believed to be written by Cao Xueqin about the Jia family.

This author wrote one poem in which the title organization collapses after Brown insults Jones after the discovery of a fossil, and bones begin to fly. "The Society upon the Stanislaus" is narrated by the title character of another poem in which Ah Sin cheats at a game he supposedly doesn't understand, sometimes called "The Heathen Chinee". This author of "Plain Language from Truthful James" wrote a poem after the death of the title literary figure describing a reading of The Old Curiosity Shop around a fire, "Dickens in Camp". This writer also wrote a short story which ends with the discovery of the body of John Oakhurst by the "law" of the title locale, and another in which the title character ironically dies in a flash flood. Name this author of The Outcasts of Poker Flat and The Luck of Roaring Camp.

One of this author's works describes an "oval O cropped out with teeth" and "the sickle motion from the thighs" of a woman about to be killed by the title character. That character also appears in "Sweeney among the Nightingales" as well as "Sweeney Erect." In another of his works, he writes that he does not know why he is "disturbing the dust on a bowl of rose-leaves," and that "If all time is eternally present / All time is unredeemable." That poem is "Burnt Norton," which is part of his Four Quartets. A more famous poem changes a nursery rhyme to "here we go round the prickly pear," and its final lines are "This is the way the world ends / Not with a bang but a whimper." His most famous poem includes Madame Sosostris with tarot cards, repeats the line "unreal city," and begins "April is the cruelest month." name this author of "The Hollow Men" and "The Waste Land."

One character in this novel stops speaking to the protagonist after he introduces a nineteen-year-old to the main female figure; that nineteen-year-old manages to fend of the attack of another figure when he discovers them together (in contrast to the protagonist, who is knocked out), and Pedro Romero refuses to shake his hand afterwards. That man in this work took up boxing to deal with the problems of being a Jew at Princeton, and both him and the protagonist fail to sustain relationships with the main female figure, although Robert Cohn remains strongly attached, and the protagonist never really gets started, since Lady Brett Ashley desires a sexual relationship. What is this novel that stars the disaffected and impotent World War I veteran Jake Barnes, by Ernest Hemingway?

In one novel by this writer, the protagonist kills a gardener who she had supposedly been falling in love with when Saburo tries to act on Etsuko's feelings, and in another work, the formerly retired Noguchi struggles with the efforts of his wealthy wife Kazu to win him an election, preferring to win on his own. In addition to Thirst for Love and After the Banquet, he wrote a short story in which the title principle is demonstrated by the protagonist, who kills himself rather than fight against the Emperor, "Patriotism", and a novel in which Mizoguchi fails to kill himself after starting a fire in the titular structure. Who is this Japanese author of The Temple of the Golden Pavilion and The Sea of Fertility tetralogy, who committed seppuku in 1970?

The complaints of Francis Topham over not receiving appointments to some ecclesiastical courts provoked one of this author's works, a satire which depicts Topham as "Trim" seeking more than his "watch-coat." In addition to A Political Romance, this author also wrote a work in which the protagonist allows a count to believe that he is the king's jester in Hamlet, allowing him to procure a passport to avoid arrest in a foreign country. This author wrote another novel with a character named Yorick, which does not discuss the birth of the title character until the fourth of nine volumes that make it up, and that title character is misnamed when Susannah is unable to tell Parson Yorick his intended name, leading to great disappointment for Walter, although Trim and Uncle Toby put less importance on it. Name this English author of A Sentimental Journey and Tristram Shandy?

One work by this man features the invention of inflatable pants as the means for the protagonist's entry into high society, where he sometimes transforms into the "Complete Man" to overcome his lack of confidence. In one novel by this author, the protagonist's friend Brian commits suicide, and Mark loses a leg on an adventure, as Anthony eventually becomes a pacifist. Mary and Mark Rampion serve as the moral compass in another one of his works as a happily married couple, in contrast to the infidelity of Marjorie Carling with her lover Walter Bidlake. In addition to writing Antic Hay and Eyeless in Gaza, this author advocated the use of LSD, depicting its religious use in Island, in contrast to the use of a fictional drug with similar effects in his most famous work. Who is this author of Point Counter Point and Brave New World?

This man wrote "Since all must judge you more unkind // I starve your body, you my mind" in "The Fair Beggar", while he also asked the title figure "Could you ascend yon' Chair of State e'er him // And snatch from there the Starry Diadem?", in "An Elegy to Princess Katherine." In addition to an ode to Charles Cotton, "The Grasshopper", this poet also addressed several poems to one figure, one of which ends with the lines "I could not love thee, Dear, so much // Loved I not honour more", and a poem whose opening line is "Stone walls do not a prison make / nor iron bars a cage." This author of "To Lucasta, Going to the Wars" is, what British poet whose most famous work is "To Althea, From Prison"?

In one short story by this author, the protagonist is shown the ravages of war by a dark bird to demonstrate the true evils of the world. That boy's quest for flowers for the burial of the dead is ultimately successful in "Strange News from Another Star", the title story in a collection by this writer. In contrast, the protagonist of another work fails, along with the other members of The League, in the title quest after the disappearance of Leo, and the protagonist of yet another novel drowns in a river after being expelled from a seminary, as Hans Giebenrath, despite his education, failed to develop personally. In addition to Journey to the East and Beneath the Wheel, this writer also wrote novels in which the high-born title character ends up as a ferryman, and Hermine teaches Harry Haller to dance. Identify this German author of Siddhartha and Steppenwolf.

This author's first novel features a protagonist who romances a nine-fingered girl in his eighteen days before going back to college. The student's friend names the series of which Hear the Wind Sing is the first; the Trilogy of the Rat by this author also includes Pinball, 1973 and A Wild Sheep Chase. A short story by this author sees the title creature confess its love for a woman, only to be killed by her imagining its torture. In addition to "The Little Green Monster", included in the collection The Elephant Vanishes, this author also wrote a novel in which Johnnie Walker tries to kill cats to make a flute, and the title character seeks his mother and sister and reads A Thousand and One Nights. The author of a novel in which Naoko's suicide drives Toru Watanabe into a wandering spell, this is, what author of Norwegian Wood and Kafka on the Shore?

The title character of one of this writer's works is only able to redeem himself after destroying Constance de Beverly to marry Clare de Clare by dying valiantly in battle. In addition to writing the epic poem Marmion, this author also inspired many musical works; in particular, an opera by Rossini inspired by a poem featuring a battle between Roderick Dhu and James Fitz-James. In addition to The Lady of the Lake, this author also wrote several novels in the Waverley series. These works include one in which the title character kills the protagonist's cousin, eventually allowing him to marry his other cousin Diana, and another, in which the title character saves the life of Rebecca, but ends up marrying Rowena. Who is this Scottish author of Rob Roy and Ivanhoe?

One of the title characters of this work is described as someone who has "belonged to any and every league that had been founded for almost any purpose whatsoever." This character, supposedly inspired by Elizabeth Peabody, suspects her doctor of "dissecting", although she still introduces Dr. Mary Prance to the male protagonist. Despite the desires of Miss Birdseye, he becomes attracted to another character after listening to her speak, even though he is strongly opposed to the actual contents of Verena Tarrant's speech. Despite the efforts of Verena's mentor, also his cousin, to win her allegiance to their movement and get her to renounce marriage, the novel ends with Verena's elopement with him. What is, this novel in which Basil Ransom wins his struggle with Olive Chancellor among the titular people, a book by Henry James?

One character in this work, instead of waiting to see his father disinherit him, ends up saving the wife of another character from rape. Celia's refusal to give herself to the title character, and Bonario's subsequent rescue, causes problems for her husband's schemes, until one of his rivals for an inheritance, the lawyer Voltore, seems to help explain away Corvino's actions with a story concocted by the title character's assistant and the appearance of Lady Politic Would-be in court; unfortunately, Mosca's story collapses spectacularly as he tries to seize the inheritance for himself. What is this play in which the title character is finally forced to give up his plot to trick his potential heirs, a comedy by Ben Jonson?

One of this writer's plays features the title character's desire towards Ferdinand, despite being married to his lover's father, while another sees the title character become wealthy after she provides an alibi (by pretending to be his mistress) for Jules Rousseau. In addition to The Stepmother, which ends in Pauline and Ferdinand's deaths, and Pamela Giraud, this author wrote a novel in which the title object shrinks under the strain of fulfilling its owner's every desire, until Raphael de Valentin dies after making love to his one true desire, and another one in which the title character dies without his two daughters that he had given everything for, instead, Eugene de Rastignac is at his deathbed. The Wild Ass' Skin and La Pere Goriot, are part of, The Human Comedy, a collection of novels by what French author?

A painting of a blindfolded woman with a lighted torch is created by one character in this work; this piece of artwork hangs in the dwelling of another character, who promises parts that never come. Despite the brickmaker's deceit, a journey eventually proceeds, although a fog and the trouble that comes with it are only repulsed by the blowing of the ship's steam whistle, an attack arranged by the intended rendezvous of the trip. At the end of this work, the captain of the ship and the narrator, to help her in her grief, lies to that character's "Intended" about his last words. Criticized by the essay "An Image of Africa" by Chinua Achebe, this is, what novella in which the last words "The horror, the horror!" are uttered by Kurtz to Marlow in the Belgian Congo, written by Joseph Conrad?

One character in this work gets the protagonist a job at the Union League Club in Chicago as a bellhop. Both Ratterer and the protagonist had held the same job at the Green-Davidson in Kansas City, until an accident that killed a little girl forced them to flee. By chance, this job leads to him meeting his wealthy uncle, who allows him to establish himself in his collar factory, where he meets the girl that will eventually prove his downfall. His plans to marry socialite Sondra Finchley go up in flames when a factory girl drowns in Big Bittern Lake after he hits her with his camera, and he is convicted the murder of the pregnant Roberta Alden. Name, this novel that ends with the execution of Clyde Griffiths, a work by Theodore Dreiser.

The picture of an exiled servant is enough for a king to fall in love, much to his wife's displeasure, in one play by this author. One poem by this author uses pairs of lovers to describe periods of time like Monsoon, Frost, and Winter, while another shows the events leading up to the title event, and the title character's killing of the demon Tarakasur. In addition to Malavika and Agnimitra, "Medley of Seasons", and "Birth of Kumara", a play by this author shows the title character being forgotten by her love, until he sees a ring that had earlier been swallowed by a fish. He also wrote a poem in which the title object is used by a banished figure to communicate with his wife. Who is this author of The Recognition of Shakuntala and "Cloud Messenger", two works in Sanskrit?

A ritual about the journey of two Navajo youths to the hogan of the Sun was described in his first published book, a collaboration with Maud Oakes, Where the Two Came to Their Father. He collaborated with Henry Morton Robinson to write A Skeleton's Key to Finnegans Wake, and he later borrowed from Finnegans Wake the name for his most important concept. He examined "primitive," "Oriental," "Occidental" and "creative" mythology in The Masks of God, but is better known for an earlier work on mythology that outlined the seventeen stages of the hero's journey. Known for a television series produced with Bill Moyers, The Power of Myth, name this scholar of comparative mythology, the author of The Hero with a Thousand Faces and the creator of the term "monomyth."

A messenger is sent to inform the title character of "an unholy, horrible thing" in this work. A command to "not unstop the wineskin's neck" convinces one character in this work to visit the title character. The title character extracts an oath from that infertile king, Aegeus, which allows the title character to give "a dress / of soft weave and a coronet of beaten gold" to another character in this story, as well as pursue an action that the nurse had previously criticized, wondering "Babes, with their father's sin? Why call thy curse on these?" That dress was made with poison which causes the deaths of the king of Corinth, Creon, and his daughter, Glauce. What is this Euripides tragedy that sees the title character kill her children to enact revenge on her husband, Jason?

Santa Battaglia tries to set up the mother of this character with a vigilant anti-Communist. Earlier, Claude Robichaux ended up getting arrested himself trying to keep this character from being arrested. Twice-offended by the flamboyant-ness of Dorian Greene, he denounces a movie as an "abortion" before having a drink at the Night of Joy Bar, where he regales all with the story of his trip on a Greyhound Scenicruiser. His dog Rex pops into his head while he is masturbating, despite this character being plagued by a broken intestinal valve. At the end of the novel in which he appears, a cockatoo tries to remove the earring worn by this lover of Myrna Minkoff under his green felt hunting cap. This fan of Dr. Nut also leads an unsuccessful workers' revolution at Levy Pants. Name this John Kennedy Toole character, the protagonist of A Confederacy of Dunces.

One event in this novel is precipitated by a dream, after which a father hears word that causes him to hide his family deeper in a cave; his failure to warn others causes him guilt for the rest of his life. It begins with the same exact dedication to Theophilus as does Luke's Gospel, but it is set apart by the controversial suggestions of a completely human Christ, a non-virgin birth, a conflict between an avaricious God and a compassionate, reluctant Christ, and a sympathetic Devil, as well as by an account of the death of St. Joseph, and multiple references to Portuguese culture. Name this controversial satire by the 1998 Nobel Prize winner Jose Saramago, which ends with Christ submitting himself to death, hoping to downplay his significance to come.
The Gospel According to Jesus Christ

He described the titular city as "branchy between towers" in his poem "Duns Scotus's Oxford". Another poem says the speaker will not "Despair, not feast on" the title entity, and another title object is predicted to "flame out, like shining from shook foil". In addition to "Carrion Comfort", another poem of his describes the title creature as "morning's minion", "daylight's dauphin", and a "dapple-dawn-drawn Falcon." Another poem of his praises "Whatever is fickle, freckled" and "skies of couple-colour as a brinded cow". That poem ends by saying "Praise him", referring to its first line, where it urged "Glory be to God for dappled things—". Identify this author of "God's Grandeur", "Pied Beauty", and "The Windhover", whose masterpiece was The Wreck of the Deutschland.

The main character in this work "[dislikes] being questioned" and "never cared for Sundays." That character kept an ad for Kruschen Salts because it amused him. After the central event in this work, the main character trains himself to remember details, including the story of the Czech, in order to pass the time. That character never even considered marrying his girlfriend until visiting Masson's bungalow. That visit was set up by the main character's relationship with Raymond Sintes. The protagonist enjoys Saturdays spent eating at Celeste's and swimming with Marie Cardona, in contrast to the work's opening scene, when he feels that "they were there to judge him", and his lack of emotion displayed at his mother's vigil would be used against him in his trial for killing an Arab. Identify this novel about Monsieur Meursault, a work by Albert Camus.

One collection of short stories by this author is set in the town of Morgana, and features members of such families as the MacLains and the Raineys, in stories like "Sir Rabbit" and "Shower of Gold". Edna Earle tells stories about Uncle Daniel in a novel by this author, while in a novella Jamie Lockhart is a bandit posing as a gentleman, in The Ponder Heart and The Robber Bridegroom respectively. One of her works follows the last hour of a man who wrecks his car near a young couple's shack, and in another work Stella Rondo runs off with Sister's boyfriend, causing her to move to the titular location. She also wrote a short story in which the protagonist must take a long journey along the Natchez Trace because of a lye-swallowing accident. Name this author of The Golden Apples, "A Worn Path", Death of a Travelling Salesman and Why I Live at the P.O.

One of this author's works includes a talking flounder taken from the Brothers' Grimm, while another prophesizes that rats will inherit the Earth. His The Citizen and his Voice contains speeches he ghost-wrote for a famous politician, whose politics he analogizes as the slow movement of a snail in From the Diary of a Snail. In one of his works, each year of a hundred is described in a short chapter told by a different narrator, and in another, Bertolt Brecht refuses to support the East Berlin workers' reformist uprising. In addition to My Century and The Plebeians Rehearse the Uprising, a more famous story concerned the sinking of the Wilhelm Gustloff, and he depicted Nazi cruelty is a trilogy that included Cat and Mouse and Dog Years. Name this German author of Crabwalk who created Oskar Matzerath in The Tin Drum.

This author wrote one short story about a demonic statuette, and another about a general whose grandson "takes over" for him with the prostitute Judith. In addition to Chac-Mool and Mother's Day, included in the collection Burnt Water, he wrote a novella in which the second person narrator falls in love with the projected younger self of his employer. In addition to Aura, the narrator of his first novel is an aspect of the god of war, and his third novel followed a group travelling from Mexico City to Veracruz; those are Where the Air is Clear and A Change of Skin. Another work sees both Phillip II construct El Escorial, as well as the cataclysmic twentieth century, while his most famous work is a recollection of a corrupt politician on his deathbed. Name this Mexican author of Terra Nostra and The Death of Artemio Cruz.

In addition to this writer's verse translations of Lucan's Pharsalia and Ovid's Elegies and Amores, his work includes a poem in which one of the title character's is mistaken for Ganymede and nearly drowned by Neptune; his version of "Hero and Leander" was finished by George Chapman. He also wrote a mostly lost play that describes the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre, in particular the misdeeds of the Duc de Guise. In one of his works, the title character poisons his daughter for becoming a Christian, and in another play, the title character strikes a 24-year deal before eternal damnation. Who is this English dramatist, author of the histories The Massacre at Paris and Edward II, and, the tragedies Doctor Faustus and The Jew of Malta?

He addressed a "daughter of Jove" and asked "Teach me to love and forgive" in one work, and he wrote that "A wondrous boy shall Rinda bear" and discussed Hoder's death in another poem. He is not Coleridge, but this author of Ode to Adversity and The Descent of Odin, wrote "Awake, Aeolian lyre, Awake" to begin another of his poems. More famously, he wrote that "where ignorance is bliss/ tis folly to be wise" in one poem, and one which begins with the line "The curfew tolls the knell of parting day." The author of odes on The Progress of Poesey, the Distant Prospect of Eton College, and the Death of a Favourite Cat, Drowned in a Tub of Goldfishes, name this author of Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.

One work by this author describes Narcissus's influence over Nero and the affect that has on Agrippa. He drew on the Old Testament for a play in which Joad and Joas lead the defeat of the titular mother of Ochiozias. In addition to Britannicus and Athalie, another of his works describes Acomat, who attempts to use the title figure and Roxane to take power away from Sultan Amurath in his Bajazet. One work by this author describes Pyrrhus marries Hermione despite his love for the titular mother of Astyanax. In another of this man's works, based on a Euripedes play and set in Troezen, Theseus eventually takes in Aricia as a daughter after Hippolytus is squashed by a sea monster. Name this French playwright of Iphegenie, Andromaque, and Phaedra.

This book opens with a statement that its events are "the black kitten's fault entirely," and an early scene is set in a garden of living flowers. The protagonist of this book is told to serve plum-cake by handing it around first, then cutting it after. That character helps a queen pin her shawl, takes Lily's place as a pawn, and dresses a pair of twins for battle after one's rattle is found ruined. Poems in this book include "The Walrus and the Carpenter," and one which the protagonist must hold up to a mirror to read. One scene in this book sees the main character visit a shop owned by a furiously knitting Sheep; there, she buys an egg that turns into Humpty Dumpty, who explains the meanings of words like "borogove" and "outgrabe." The Lion and the Unicorn, Red and White Queens, and Tweedledum and Tweedledee, all appear in, which book, the sequel to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland?

This man retold the Robinson Crusoe story in his Foe, and described a dying former professor named Mrs. Curren who is tended to by Vercueil in Age of Iron. Another work by this man describes Magda, who kills her father and has an affair with a workman. He wrote about Colonel Joll who tortures people in an effort to find information about the title figures of another book, appalling the Magistrate. Another character created by this man takes his mother Anna's ashes to a farm in Karoo after being raised in a home for disabled people because of his harelip. Name this South African author of In the Heart of the Country, Waiting for the Barbarians and The Life and Times of Michael K.

In one short story by this author, a French letter from Elise is translated by an unnamed narrator for Maggie Goytes, who loves Joey, the titular bird. In addition to that short story, this author wrote a novel in which the protagonist leaves his wife Lottie so he can have "perfect singleness," only to be seduced by the former fiancée of Jim Bricknell. Josephine Ford's seduction of him leads that character to eventually destroy the titular flute. Another novel by this author sees the protagonist quickly become attached to the older and married Clara Dawes and at the end of the novel, Gertrude Morel dies. In another novel by this author of The Plumed Serpant and the "Odour of Chrysanthemums," the titular character's husband had a crippling injury causing him to use a motorized wheelchair, sexually frustrating Connie. Name this British author of Aaron's Rod, Sons and Lovers and Lady Chatterley's Lover.

In one work this author details the life of a tomb-maker who makes extra money by playing the organ at an insane asylum, while another of his novels sees Swartz give a refugee proper documentation only after he tells him his life story in the title Portuguese city. In addition to The Black Obelisk and The Night in Lisbon, he also wrote about Robert and Otto selling their auto workshop and visiting Patrice in a Swiss tuberculosis sanatorium in his novel The Three Comrades, while the turbulent life of the German surgeon Ravic is told in The Arch of Triumph. Another of his novels, The Road Back, is thought to be a sequel to his most famous book, in which the patriotic teacher Kantorek convinces Paul Bäumer and his friends to join the Germany Army during World War I. Name this German author who wrote All Quiet on the Western Front.

He wrote a criticism of a hypocritical priest in "The Jamaica Funeral" and an allegory on death entitled "The House of Night." The co-author of the satirical Father Bombo's Pilgrimage to Mecca, he is also known describing the discovery of America in "Pictures of Columbus" and for introducing an early version of Manifest Destiny in his epic poem "The Rising Glory of America." Those works, however, are not as famous as one that uses the lines "And long shall timorous fancy see / The painted chief, and pointed spear" to describe the titular cemetery, one about the imminent death of a flower, or one about the author's six-week stay on a British prison ship. Name this poet who wrote the poems "The Wild Honey Suckle" and "The Indian Burial Ground" and is often known by his nickname, "Poet of the American Revolution."

Billy Kirby kills maple trees to get their sap, and the townspeople waste thousands of fish by letting them rot on the shores of Lake Otsego in the first published book in this series. That novel was only the fourth chronologically; in the third, the protagonist of the series falls in love with Mabel Dunham, only to lose her to Jasper, and in the first, he uses chess pieces found in a chest to help the "daughters" of Thomas Hutter ransom him from the Hurons. That novel, set before The Pathfinder, was criticized for committing 114 out of a possible 115 "offenses against literary art" by Mark Twain. The Pioneers and The Deerslayer are two works in, this series of five novels featuring Natty Bumppo, the second of which is The Last of the Mohicans, written by James Fenimore Cooper?

The action of this work begins after one character is told to bring the jewelry of the protagonist to Ancona, while in another scene the spouse of the protagonist drops a horoscope, revealing that he is about to have a son. One character in this work kills his mistress Julia, the wife of Castruchio, with a poisoned Bible after telling of his involvement in the central murder plot, while three others, including Cariola, are killed along with the title character. Daniel de Bosola kills the title character under the orders of Ferdinand in this work, due to the potential loss of inheritance. Name this play whose title character is killed after marrying the lowly steward Antonio, a Restoration drama by John Webster.

This man's book-length analysis of Les Miserables is entitled The Temptation of the Impossible. One of this man's works is a biograph of Paul Gaughin and Flora Tristan, and recounts their meeting in Tahiti. Another novel by this author concerns Ricardo's lifelong obsession with an immigrant named Lily, who treats him as a bland interlude between her numerous affairs with increasingly powerful men. Besides The Way To Paradise and Bad Girl, this author recounts Cava's theft of the answer key to a chemistry exam on behalf of The Circle, a group of cadets at the Leoncio Prado Military Academy. Another of his novels has alternating chapters about Pedro Camacho and a protagonist that falls in love with his uncle's sister in law, who are all employees of a radio station. Name this author of The Time of the Hero and Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter.

The narrator of this poem compares bine-stems to the strings of broken lyres in the opening of this work, which also describes wind as a "death-lament". The narrator describes his surroundings as "The Century's corpse outlent/his crypt the cloudy canopy" and also states that "every spirit upon earth/seemed fervourless as I". All mankind "sought their household fires" on the night of this poem, whose title figure decided to "fling his soul/upon the growing gloom". The title figure's sound "was written on terrestrial things" and "trembled through/his happy good night air". Opening with the narrator leaning upon a coppice gate before viewing the title animal, which is described as "aged […], frail, gaunt, and small", name this poem by Thomas Hardy about a bird.

At one point in this poem, the speaker says: "Look at me from the depths of the earth, tiller of fields, weaver, reticent shepherd." This is after the poet has asked himself what the "indestructable, the imperishable, life" is earlier in the work. At another point the speaker states "many deaths come to each, every day a little death." Shortly after this, the poet arrives at the title locale, the "stellar void of the final steps of vertingous spiraling road." The poem ends with the lines "cling to my body like magnets, hasten to my veins and to my mouth, speak through my words and through my blood," addressed to the dead builders of the titular site, earlier urged to "Rise up to be born with me." Coming after "A Lamp on Earth" in its poet's Canto General, name this second part of a poetic history of the Americas by Pablo Neruda, named for an ancient Incan site.

In this play, one character enters and notes that she has recently read the paper. Two other characters at the time note that they have been waiting for hours to eat and are quite hungry, before finding out that their guests have been waiting for them outside the whole time. Later, those four characters have a heated exchange including such lines as "you can sit on the chair if it hasn't got any," "Scaramoushe," and "It is not that way, it's over here." The hosts realize that they are husband and wife while talking to each other. A fire chief, as he leaves the party, mentions the titular character, which puts a chill on the whole dinner, but who is otherwise never mentioned. At the end of this play, the Martins switch places with the Smiths as the curtain goes down. Name this piece of the theater of the absurd, a work about a titular singer and the first play of Eugene Ionesco.

The first and last alliterative lines of this work state that it takes place it after the siege of Troy, and Adam, Solomon, Samson, and David are listed as exemplars by one character in this work, who praises the idea of loving women, but not trusting them. One character in this work encourages his guests to try to get a hood placed on a spear, in a game which parallels this work's central plot. The two title characters of this work agree to exchange their winnings for three days, earning one many kisses, but the failure of one character to give up an enchanted belt results in that character receiving a cut on his neck, when the title characters meet again at a chapel to finish another game. Attributed to the Pearl Poet, this is, what work which features a beheading-game between a knight of the Round Table and a colorful warrior?
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

In one work by this author, Donatello may not be completely human and Miriam is being sought after by a Model, and Kenyon is a humanist sculptor. The title character of another of his works goes to a meeting place where he is led by the devil, who shows that all of the seemingly Christian members of his town are actually Satanists. In another short story, Colonel Killigrew and Mr. Meadbourne drink water of the fountain of youth. In one novel by this author, Holgrave Maude and Phoebe Pynchon defy their ancestral conflicts and fall in love, while Clifford and Hepzibah are freed from the specter of their ancestor, a judge who presided over the Salem Witch Trials. In addition to The Marble Faun, he collected "Young Goodman Brown" and "Dr. Heidegger's Experiment" in Twice-Told Tales. Name this author of the House of the Seven Gables and The Scarlet Letter.

In one scene in this work, a rebuke against blasphemers interrupts a conversation, which causes everyone to be stupefied. That sets up the stage for a story in which two characters are given a temple where their old home once stood. In another story in this work, a mixup involving a lion causes one character to stab himself, painting some mulberries red. This work opens with an account of the creation of the universe, which is followed by the four ages of man. Another story is that of a man who believes that "though Minos may close in the land and sea, the sky yet lies open" but who comes to tragedy when his son ignores his lesson and flies too close to the sun. Those other aforementioned stories are Salamacis and Hermanthophoditus, Pyramus and Thisbe, Philemon and Baucis and Daedalus and Icarus. Name this mock-epic poem about "forms changed," a work of Ovid.

This character gained pivotal information by reading a newspaper article by Cuvier, and as a child he had great success playing his friends in a game called Odds and Evens. In one story centering on this protagonist, the title character was working for Monsieur Le Blanc, while in another he intentionally leaves behind a snuff box in the office of the antagonist. That same story reveals how he was slighted in Vienna by the antagonist, but is able to get revenge on Minister D by switching the titular object with a duplicate. He has frequent interactions with a prefect known only by the initial G, and in his first appearance, he figured out that Madame L'Espanaye and her daughter were killed by an orangutan. Also appearing in "The Mystery of Marie Roget" and "The Purloined Letter", name this recurring detective in Edgar Allen Poe stories like "The Murders in the Rue Morgue".

One scene in this work sees patrons of Hartman's Cafe berate Postmistress Clare for a comment she made to the Telegram. One character in this book likes to run over dogs on the road for fun and hangs out with a character who recounts how got pneumonia due to a nurse at a foster home putting him in a cold tub to cure him of his chronic bed wetting. That latter character had earlier lied about killing a man in Las Vegas. Bobby Rupp is devastated by the central action in this book, from which Eveanna and Beverly are partially spared. The central action in this work took place thanks to a tip given by Floyd Wells about a safe kept by the father of Nancy and Kenyon, and it ends with the execution of Dick Hickock and Perry Smith. Name this account of the murder of the Clutter Family by Truman Capote.

One of this man's poems reflects on an octopus looking at the moon, while he also wrote a work of comparative literary criticism of two poets in which he judges the poems and chooses the winner, which is titled after a children's game. His early works, such as "Green Peach", were written as an homage to Li Po. This author of "Record of a Weather-Exposed Skeleton" and "The Seashell Game" also wrote a fictionalized account of his travels with his companion Sora from Edo to Oku, The Narrow Road to the Deep North. The author of a poem about a frog jumping into an ancient pond, identify this Edo period master of haiku, whose penname comes from the plantain tree.

"Memory" is blamed for the three-volume novels that Mudie keeps sending a character in this work, a girl who later notes "the weather still continues charming" in a letter she wrote to herself breaking off an imaginary engagement. Minor characters in this play include the servants Merriman and Lane, while one of the male leads gets his surname from the destination of the man that found him in a handbag in Victoria Station. Another character constantly gets out of engagements by claiming to care for a fictional invalid named Bunbury, and both of the male leads get Reverend Canon to christen them. The two central women in this play are governed by Miss Prism and the snobbish Lady Bracknell. Seeing both Cecily Cardew and Gwendolen Fairfax infatuated with the titular name, name this play centering on John Worthing and Algernon Moncrieff, written by Oscar Wilde.

Willa Cather's essay "148 Charles Street" describes her first meeting with this writer and her Boston-marriage partner, Annie Fields. One of this author's novels depicts the growing friendship between Helen Denis and Kate Lancaster, who visit the title town. Besides Deephaven, this author set her tale of Nan Prince's upbringing by the title character as an independent-minded young woman in the same state. However, A Country Doctor does not take place in this author's fictional town of Dunnet Landing, setting of many stories and her novel in which Mrs. Todd represents life on the land and Captain Littlepage life on the sea. Also author of a short story in which Sylvy refuses the hunter's bribe of ten dollars and a knife to provide the whereabouts of the title bird, for 10 points who is this author of The Country of Pointed Firs and "A White Heron"?

The exploits of the Spanish heroes Rengo, Tucapel, and Lautaro are recounted by Alonso de Ercilla in this nation's founding epic, La Araucana. Creacionismo was a Modernist literary movement created in Paris by a poet from this country, Vicente Huidobro. A more recent novelist from this nation wrote the memoir The Boom in Spanish-American Literature: A Personal History, as well as a novel in which the narrator Humberto takes on various guises, including The Mute and El Imbunche, while ostensibly telling the story of the deformed Boy, whose father Jeronimo surrounds him with freaks so he'll seem normal. Along with the author of The Obscene Bird of Night, Jose Donoso, this nation also produced the author of Crepusculario and Residence on Earth, as well as a collection of poems that includes "Tonight I Can Write." For 10 points this is what nation, home to Pablo Neruda?

The reader is advised to "take the lively air" in this poem, as "Great Nature has another thing to do/To you and me." The speaker exclaims, "God bless the ground! I shall walk softly there," and he "hear[s] his being dance from ear to ear." A critical factor in one's interpretation of this poem is whether the repeated words "to sleep" are read as an infinitive or prepositional phrase. The poet breaks the rules of the villanelle form in the odd numbered stanzas by not exactly repeating the last line of the first stanza, "I learn by going where I have to go." What is this poem that titles a 1953 collection by its author, Theodore Roethke, in which the speaker "wake[s] to sleep" and takes the title action slow?

This author outlines his theories of sexual warfare in the essay "On Psychic Murder," applications of which can be found in minor dramas like The Creditor and Pariah. One of this author's novels revolves around an idealistic civil servant whose experiences depict the author's own bohemian lifestyle as a member of a coterie of artists that met at the namesake restaurant. In one of his "chamber plays" for his so-called "tiny theatre" an Old Man assigns a student to attend a performance of "The Valkyrie." That student, Arkenholz passes by a building which contains a statue of a woman worshipped by a Mummy who lives inside. Author of The Red Room, Master Olof and A Dream Play, name this Swedish playwright of The Ghost Sonata.

The line, "in this world, only the heart of man is vile," is quoted exactly four times in this novel, which is attributed to the Confucian thinker Xun Zi. One of the central characters in this novel dies from an accidental overdose of aphrodisiac pills. Though it is not the Water Margin, in this novel, an eight-foot tall figure who is known for killing an attacking tiger with his bare hands avenges his brother Wu Da Lang's death and another similarity involves the seduction of Pan Jinlian. Taking its title from the three central female characters; it chronicles the downfall of the Ximen family during the Northern Song Dynasty. Written under the pseudonym "The Scoffing Scholar of Lan-ling," name this rather sexually graphic Chinese Novel by Langling Xiaoxiao Sheng.
The Plum in the Golden Vase

One elegy in this work is dedicated to a noble knight who "wore the Crown of Bayes," and lived "When England did injoy her Halsion dayes," and was ultimately slain at the Seige of Zutphon. Anticipating the criticism this work would receive the author in the prologue notes, "I am obnoxious to each carping tongue/Who says my hand a needle better fits." The last commendatory verses include a set of anagrams of the author's name like "Artes bred neate An." The lines "Thou ill-form'd offspring of my feeble brain" appear in the second edition and the section "The Four Monarchies" was appended to the quaternions. Written "By a Gentlewoman in those Parts," name this collection, which contains such poems as "The Author to Her Book," written by Anne Bradstreet.
The Tenth Muse, Lately Sprung Up in America

While a member of the Semi-Colon club, a literary group in Cincinnati, this author did publish a number of short stories in Godey's Lady's Book. In one short-story by this author Giuletta is advised that "Eagles make bad work in dove-cots" regarding a certain cavalier with whom she flirts and Girolamo Savonarola is an important character in this author's "Agnes of Sorrento." Though this author is not Lillian Hellman, this author did write a work Little Foxes under the pen name Christopher Crowfield. In one of this author's novels, Ophelia Sinclaire, the cousin of Augustine, takes her to task for defending a certain institution and the title character at one point tries to write based on the instructions he received from Mas'r George. Name this American author whose little anti-slavery book started a war according to Abraham Lincoln.

One of the central characters in this play claims that the other was "the Pope and the Holy Office and the Inquisition all rolled into one," when it came to their work. Throughout this play, the characters editorialize from the afterlife, and when one claims he suffered, Margrethe retorts "On your hands and knees? It's my husband who's on his hands and knees," referring to the fact that her husband had to be smuggled out to Sweden. The play ends noting "no more uncertainty, because there's no more knowledge" regarding the central event then one of the characters appropriately notes that there is always uncertainty. Written by the author of Democracy and Noises Off, name this 2000 Tony Award winning play by Michael Frayn about a 1941 meeting between Werner Heisenberg and Niels Bohr.

The narrator in one work with this title notes that people were stealing shoe laces and polish out of each other's hand in the section "Looting is a lot of fun, but you have to know how to do it." In another work with this title, the speaker sees himself as Alfred Dreyfus and refers to his persecutors as "Philistines." In that work's the author imagines a relationship between Anne Frank and Peter van Pels. In the novel with this title, Dina Pronicheva, an actress with the Kiev Puppet Theatre, is forced to walk to a ravine, undress and then is shot but manages to survive. That novel is subtitled, "A Document in Novel Form." One work with this title was written by the author of Wild Berries and "Kazan University." name this title shared by an Alexander Kuznetsov novel, and a symphony by Dmitri Shostakovich based on a poem by Yevgeny Yevtushenko.

When a central character in this work, a doctor, discovers that his rival will be marrying Helena, he notes in his diary that he feels as "if flames of ice were suffocating me," a pointed reference to Dante's Inferno. That character attempts to manipulate his rival's child into following his career path, a son also named after the doctor. One character play-acts the throttling of another, though this results in the immediate death of that character as he has a weak heart. This novella is often paired with two other stories "The Madness of Dr. Montarco" and "San Manuel the Good, Martyr." Criticisms of this work note that the two central characters' names invoke a biblical story of envy and at the end of the novel Joaquin offers his deathbed confession. Written by the author of Niebla, name this novel about the titular painter by Miguel Unamuno.

The first novel in a loosely connected trilogy ending with the posthumously published Whistle and including The Thin Red Line, name this 1952 American novel by James Ramon Jones, also turned into a 1953 Award winning film starring Montgomery Clift as Private Prewitt.

This author attempted a definition of "genius" in his essay about street performers, "The Indian Jugglers." His work subtitled "The New Pygmalion," a thinly veiled description of his attempts to seduce Sarah Walker, provoked much outrage. That book, Liber Amoris, preceded another scandalous work, an essay in first person depicting this author's visit to an illegal bare-knuckles boxing match titled "The Fight." That essay was collected with other pieces, including the essay in which he describes reading Lyrical Ballads in manuscript, "My First Acquaintance with the Poets," and his "On the Pleasure of Hating," in the collection Table Talk. Known for his personal and casual style, in contrast to his friend Charles Lamb, for 10 points who was this Romantic-era author of The Spirit of the Age?

One of this author's poems notes, "Necessity makes people err, And hunger drives the wolf from the woods." Two lines from one of this man's poems were adapted in a Berthold Brecht poem set to music by Hans Eisler and Kurt Weil for the work, The Roundheads and the Pointedheads. In that poem, "Nannas Lied" Brecht kept this author's interrogative but changed the time frame. The lines by this author written while he awaited his execution, "Brothers, men who live after us, Let not your hearts be hardened against us," are used to open Truman Capote's In Cold Blood. Author of "Ballad of the Hanged Men," name this medieval French poet who wonders, "Where are the snows of yesteryear?" in "Ballad of the Dead Ladies," and wrote The Great Testament.

In one section of this novel, "His Life until the Age of 12" relates the wrongful arrest of his father for the theft of Murray's heifer and an odd accusation of tranvestism made against the central character. Though fictional, the author of this work attempted to mimic the writing style of its central character as evinced by Jerilderie Letter, and thus outside the frame narrative "S.C," the novel proper contains no commas. Consisting of 13 sections, each ostensibly written by the central character, after that character and his love Mary Hearn rob two banks successfully, she emigrates to San Francisco, while he and the title group are betrayed by Thomas Curnow and are cornered in Glenrowan located in Victoria. Name this Booker-prize winning historical novel about an Australian bushranger and outlaw, written by Peter Carey.
True History of the Kelly Gang

One poem by this author discusses "watching tired housewives" who try "to fight off/their beer-maddened husbands." Another poem by him mentions "a tomb of a room/without cigarettes." In addition to "And The Moon And The Stars And The World" and "Poem For My 43rd Birthday," Ecco Publishing has released a number of new volumes by this poet including The Flash of Lightning Behind the Mountain. He castigates poets, poetry and himself in "B as in Bullshit," and a novel by him is about a man who searches Los Angeles for a job. In addition to Pulp, another work follows the same protagonist and his love Jane Conney Baker, known as "Betty." name this author who included Henry Chinaski in works like Post Office, Factotum and Ham on Rye.

He wrote about the effect that a convert had on the local villagers in one novel, while the real-estate investor Boris' Upper West Side party is attended by a number of academics including Professor Shrage and Halperin, whose moustache made him look like Nietzsche. In addition to Shadows on the Hudson, his interest in vegetarianism can be seen in works like The Slaughterer, and he wrote another novel in which the title character is the daughter of Bashele and Zelig and is loved by a writer named Aaron Gredinger, who is nicknamed Tsutsik, and is titled Shosha. This author's first published novel focuses on two characters who commit adultery on the eve of Yom Kippur. Name this author of Satan in Goray and The Family Moskat, a Yiddish-language Nobel laureate from Poland.

In the sixth section of this poem, the speaker comforts the reader by saying "the dark threw its patches down upon me also," and in the fifth section, the speaker admits that the "curious abrupt questionings stir within me." This poem includes four consecutive lines that begin with the word "Just," including "Just as any of you is one of a living crowd, I was one of a crowd." That section also describes some seagulls, whom the speaker saw "high in the air / floating with motionless wings, oscillating their bodies." Originally published as "Sun-Down Poem" in the second edition of Leaves of Grass, this poem begins "Flood-tide below me! I see you face to face." name this poem by Walt Whitman that describes his thoughts while going "from shore to shore" on a boat.

In this work, some believe that their lost things go to Norfolk. Some characters set off from the Kingsfield to see a beached boat and the "tokens controversy" arises when some characters demand remuneration for artwork that is meant to see if students have souls. Another character looks at the faces in porn magazines because she believes she is "modeled on trash." This novel's title comes from a Judy Bridgewater song the narrator is singing when Madame catches her dancing with a pillow. "Completing" is a euphemism for death in this work. Hailsham is the setting for much of this work that speaks of Ruth and Tommy's donations. Kathy H. Is a "carer" in this novel about clones used for organ donation. Identify this novel by Kazuo Ishiguro.

In a David Wagoner poem, this man's "white-on-white shirt and tie were luminous" and his trousers were "creased like knives to the tops of his shoes." This man was given kangaroo-tendon cheekbones in an operation performed by Wilhelm Loeser, and he once escaped from jail using a wooden gun blackened with shoe polish. Billie Frechette was the girlfriend of this man, who was the subject of a meeting between a Hungarian brothel owner known as the Woman in Red, and Melvin Purvis, an FBI agent. After watching the movie Manhattan Melodrama, this gangster was killed outside the Biograph Theater in Chicago in 1934. Name this bank robber who was played by Johnny Depp in the 2009 film Public Enemies.

One of this author's poems says "the [blues waves] dance and tremble" and "the mast bends." In another poem, he describes seafoam rolling like "white pearls of desire" down the cheeks of a girl "born to the King of the Tide," though her fishy tail bakes in the sun. This poet of "The Sail" relates a theme of "The Princess of the Tide" to a work in which a young Circassian boy flees from a monastery. Another one of his poems describes a fight between the oprichnik Kirbeevich and the titular man. This author of "The Novice" and "The Song of the Merchant Kalashnikov" is probably best known for a work which contains the section "Princess Mary." identify this author who wrote about the Byronic Pechorin in A Hero of Our Time.

In one of this man's ironically titled short stories, a woman accidently falls off a step ladder while carrying an unborn child named Crispin, whose father had died. In addition to "Life Doesn't Take Itself Very Seriously," another story by this author, which is narrated by the sibling of Tacha, describes the loss of a cow during a flood. That story along with "No Dogs Bark" and "Tell them Not to Kill Me" appear in a collection, whose titular story depicts the violent yet respected Pedro Zamora. In one of this man's works, a young man is sent by Abundio to the home of Dona Eduviges to find out about the title character. Written by the author of The Golden Cock and Other Film Scripts, that highly-fragmented novel describes Juan Precadio's journey to Comala, a ghost town. Name this Mexican author of The Burning Plain and Other Stories and Pedro Paramo.

A scheme by the title character of this work involves getting some nobles drunk and tricking them into signing an oath of loyalty to him. The title character's demise is eventually engineered by Colonel Butler, after which the title character's daughter, Thekla, flees Egra, where the murder occurs. An investigation into the loyalty of this work's title character is begun by the commissioner Von Questenburg, and this work's title character at one point negotiates for the Hungarian crown. At the end of this play, Max Piccolomini is killed while fighting the Swedes, while his father, Octavio Piccolomini, is elevated to the princehood by the emperor, who had feared the military supremacy of the title character. Consisting of three plays, identify this historical drama in which the titular duke of Friedland is assassinated despite his success in prosecuting the Thirty Years' War, written by Friedrich Schiller.

In one section of this work, "Paul's Church," is said to not be more safe than "Paul's Churchyard," from "Bookful blockhead... With loads of learned lumber in his head." One line in this poem describes nature as "unerring," and "still divinely bright," and claims that "rules of old... Are nature methodized," while in another section, "young Maro" finds that Nature and Homer are the same. In this work, practitioners of the title discipline are enjoined to "be silent always when you doubt your sense." This poem opens with the line "‘Tis hard to say if greater want of skill/ Appear in writing or in judging ill," and contains the famous commandment to "drink deep or taste not the Pierian Spring," because "A little Learning is a dang'rous thing." identify this didactic poem about evaluating art, written by Alexander Pope.

One story by this author features a woman who lives with her brother and knits continuously, causing clothing to pile up around the house. That story also sees the title event, which causes the protagonists to seal off rooms until they are left on the street. This author also wrote a story which sees a wealthy man read about a murder plot between a woman and her paramour, who turn out to be the man's wife and her lover. This author also wrote about a man recovering from a motorcycle accident who dreams he is a Motecan Indian pursued by Aztec warriors, only to realize that the dream is reality. Name this author of "The House Taken Over," "Continuity of Parks," and "The Night Face Up" who included such stories in his collections The End of the Game and Bestiary.

Arabic does not have distinct forms for this noun case, but instead uses the prefix "li". In Classical Greek, this noun case can serve five different functions, including indicating the possessor of an object or the purpose of an action. In Latin third declension i-stem nouns, this case is marked by a long i, and its Latin third person reflexive pronoun was "sibi". This noun case is one of two that has distinct forms in German but not in English. Romance languages like Spanish exhibit separate forms for this case only in pronouns, while in English this case is marked by the preposition "to" in front of a noun. Name this noun case used for indirect objects.

This character is described as always "sowing broadcast the dragon's teeth" in creating imaginary enemies "against whom she rushed to battle." One scene sees this chracter pointing across a brook while her reflection does the same is noted by Anne Marie McNamara in her work about this figure, which is entitled The Character of Flame That incident also sees this character wash off a kiss in that brook and later note how strange that another figure talks with her mother while sitting on a heap of moss in the deep forest, but pretends not to know them among all of the people. One incident sees this child hold hands with her parents while they stand on the town scaffold and watch a comet blaze across the sky. Name this embodiment of an object worn by Hester Prynne, her daughter.

A character in this work gets fake papers, which describes him as a dealer of barometers. After a character in this work is betrayed to the Austrian police, his banishment decree was modified by the Baron Binder, which demanded that he eschew all reading material written after 1720 except for the novels of Sir Walter Scott. After being arrested, the jailer's wife is able to conceal that character and provide him with the belongings of a soldier who had been arrested for stealing a cow and some silver spoons. Aunt Gina and Count Mosca try to assist the main character in this novel by sending him to seminary in Naples. The central character, an ardent admirer of Napoleon who grew up near Lake Como, ends up fighting at Waterloo. Name this novel about the life and adventures of Fabrice del Dongo, who ends up becoming a monk in the title establishment by Stendhal.

Though it's not The Maids, a wind-up clock in this work allows characters to act out imaginary events, and one character claims he "can wrap up in the smell of" another when he dons his overcoat. One character in this play soaks his feet nightly in bath salts because he has footsore from his job as a gatekeeper at the zoo, and at the climax, that character spends his life savings on a suit instead of saving to buy a farm. One scene sees two characters play roles in apartheid and nearly come to blows. Those two characters invite a white pen pal to Port Elizabeth, but that woman, Ethel Lange, gets married and never visits. Name this play about light-skinned Morris and dark-skinned Zachariah by Athol Fugard in which the title object is the bond between brothers.

One of this man's works was inspired by an incident where two priests murdered a London Justice named Sir Edmondsbury Godfrey. That work focuses on two girls ditching their squire fiancés and getting married to Yorkshire gentlemen, while the corrupt titular priest performs a fake exorcism on Sir Edward Hartford. In addition to writing The Amorous Bigot, another work by this author sees a supposedly virtuous character brag about all the love letters and gifts she acquires as a prostitute. Mrs. Jilt, ends up marrying the Clodplate, the protagonist of Epsom Wells. He appears as the King of Nonsense in The Dunciad, and as the character Og in Absalom and Acitophel. Name this English author who was presented as a "True Blue Protestant Poet" in Mac Flecknoe.

One character has a tradition of giving chocolate to the girl's pool, and another claims to be dumber than an eight year old because she doesn't know what a charlatan is. The crazy Knowles operates the mayonnaise elevator number five. Hazels' obsession with Hoosiers is an example of a false karass, while the ambassador Horlick and his wife Claire represented a duprass; Horlick was later fired for his comments regarding Americans. Frank, who stages bug fights and was known as secret agent X-9, and Newt, who is shorter than an umbrella stand, are the sons of Dr. Hoenikker, whose central invention of the novel was originally developed for marines. Featuring the banana republic of San Lorenzo and the religion of Bokononism, name this Vonnegut novel about ice-nine, which takes its name from a string game played by Dr. Hoenikker.

In a translation of this poem, J.B. Leishman included the line "His gaze...is so misted with tiredness," though he is sometimes contrasted with a more plodding translator Edward Snow who described one figure in this poem with the line "his gaze...holds nothing anymore." A translation by Leonard Cottrell describes "a noble will that stands there numb" and describes that prisoner with the line "along a nerve, awareness darts - arriving in his heart, it dies." The translation by Robert Bly describes the exhibit as "bars, a hundred thousand bars, and behind the bars, nothing." Composed at Rodin's advice after a trip to the Jardin des Plantes, name this Rilke poem about a big cat.

One author from this country wrote a story about a girl forced into prostitution because a storm washed away her cow, titled Because We Are So Poor. Another author from this country wrote a novel in which the protagonist breaks a curse imposed by her tyrannical mother preventing her from marrying; that work is divided into 12 chapters each beginning with a recipe. Yet another author from this country is studied in The Traps of Faith and wrote a play in which Human Nature allegorizes Christ as the title figure. In addition to being the home of the authors of those works, Like Water for Chocolate and The Divine Narcissus, a famous collection of essays about this country includes "The Sons of La Malinche" and "The Pachuco and other Extremes." name this country whose national character is described in The Labyrinth of Solitude, a work by Octavio Paz.

One play whose English title ends with this word features a pastor who is constantly followed around by his twelve daughters and is named Straw Man. That play, whose title ends with this word, is about a pair that decides not to get married in order to avoid spoiling a perfect romance. A trilogy whose title ends with this word concludes with Fleur being saved from an art gallery fire and was followed by The End of the Chapter. In addition to a play about Falk and Svanhild entitled "love's" this, by Henrik Ibsen, and the "modern" follow-up trilogy to The Forsyte Saga by John Galsworthy, this word describes a play in which the merchant Aegeon is ransomed from a death sentence and two servants named Dromio are confused. Give this word that describes a Shakespeare play about a meeting in Ephesus between a pair of twins named Antipholus, which leads to many "errors."

A Married Man's Story was unfinished at the point of the author's death. This author identified with the dying singing canary of her last work whereas at the end of another work, a dove's cry is mirrored in the shouts of the name Reggie as he leaves Anne. One of this writer's story concerns an older fat stranger who remarks that Lelia's pretty arms will eventually turn into "little short fat ones" during Her First Ball. Frau Brechenmacher Attends a Wedding and The Sister of the Baroness are some stories in the New Age that would be published in 1911 in her first collection In a German Pension. Name this writer from New Zealand who wrote The Fly, Miss Brill, and The Garden Party.

Selina Hines recently published a biography on "the secret lives" of this author. The author's lovers Alan Searle and Gerald Haxton probably disapproved of the statement that, "the homosexual has small power of invention, but a wonderful gift for delightful embroidery." One of this author's short stories, the basis of the silent film Sadie Thompson, tells of a missionary's attempt to save a fallen woman who has moved to Pago Pago. He reused elements from that short story "Rain," in a novel about the painter Charles Strickland who becomes blinded by leprosy after he moves to Tahiti. The collection The Casuarina Tree includes such stories as the "Before the Party" and "P and O." name this author of The Moon and Sixpence and Of Human Bondage.

This novel has a dialogue wherein "The Voice" explains to "Beauty" that she will spend fifteen years as a "susciety girl." The protagonist tells a tale of the imaginary Chevalier O'Keefe to his fling Geraldine Burke, and also carries on an affair with Dorothy Raycroft before failing out of officer's training camp. That protagonist is beaten up by Joseph Black, who had changed his name from Joseph Bloeckman, while this novel sees Maury Noble end up wealthy and Dick Caramel end as a successful though hack writer. Despite being disinherited for his drunken parties, the protagonist ends the novel quite wealthy along with his wife Gloria. Name this novel about Anthony Patch by F. Scott Fitzgerald.

The speaker reads in a "light Mosaick" and mentions "strange prophecies my Phancy weaves/And in one History consumes." After "retiring from the Flood," this work's speaker lets himself "imbark/in this yet green, and growing Ark" and it ends with the "salmon-fishers" as "rational Amphibii." It describes a girl who desires "Heaven's dialect" named Maria as well as some nuns whose "loudw'st cannon were their lungs" when Isabel Thwaites is rescued from the convent. She goes on to father a hero who "laid these gardens out in sport/In the just figure of a Fort." Opening "Within this sober Frame expect/Work of no Forrain Architect," name this poem about the home of Thomas Fairfax by Andrew Marvell.

In one of this man's poems, the smell of the title substance reminds a man of "the big/house he visited when he was eight," but "the mallet slipped long since from the hands…that are not the hands of a child." This author of "Soap Suds" wrote, "Let them not make me a stone and let them not spill me/otherwise kill me" in a poem that begins "I am not yet born; O hear me." One of this man's comic poems begins by asserting, "It's no go the merry-go-round, it's no go the rickshaw." name this author of "Prayer Before Birth" and "Bagpipe Music," an Irish poet who was friends with W.H. Auden and Stephen Spender.

The narrator of this novel receives a postcard decorated with a Little Red Riding Hood cartoon. After a forehead injury, the main character has experiences of appearing to be dead but then would come back to life after peeing; he later suffers from amnesia and daydreams about murder. He remembers the night-soil man, the Joan of Arc picture book, the odor of sweat, and the carrying of the shrine. That character has a sexual encounter with a painting of St. Sebastian and becomes fixated with the armpits of Omi. He almost marries Sonoko and goes to a brothel whereupon he hopes to die in a B-29 bombing raid. Name this novel in which Kochan metaphorically hides behind the titular item, written by Yukio Mishima.

One character in this novel dreams about an organ "like a golden city upon the side of a mountain" and is told that "it is Handel." Later, that character is involved in a balloon crash, but is rescued by captain Giovanni Gianni. That character runs into problems marrying his love, because her elder daughter Zulora must marry first. A watch is confiscated because the people who have seemingly swapped the ideas of illness and crime also believe that machines would evolve and take over. The main character marries the daughter of Nosnibor, Arowhena after escaping over the mountains from the land he set off with Chowbok. Name this Samuel Butler novel centering on Higgs's travels to the titular satire of Victorian England.

In one of this author's stories, the titular girl is inspired and later disillusioned by the charismatic King Barlo. This author wrote about a "dynamic atom aggregate" in an 835-line poem ending, "Let the big light in!" In another of this man's short stories, Bob Stone carries on an affair with Louisa, but finds him with Tom Burwell, who kills him and is lynched. This man wrote a play in which Ralph returns from New York to teach in the South, but needs help from Fred Halsey and the former slave Father John. This author collected "Blood-Burning Moon" and "Kabnis" in a volume of African-American poetry, stories, and plays. Name this Harlem Renaissance author of Cane.

In this work, two characters discuss Constance, who was called "old" by a Portuguese man, but thought he meant "pretty." At the end of this work, the title character is served a dish of tarantulas and vipers with wine made of vinegar and ice. The title character of this work puts on the cape of the Marques de la Mota and takes the places of Batricio and Don Octavio. Accompanied by his reluctant servant Catalinon, the title character betrays the lower-class women Tisbea and Aminta. At this play's climax, Don Gonzalo punishes the title character for his deceptions by dragging him to hell. Name this drama about the playboy Don Juan, written by Tirso de Molina.

This character insists that a cook purchase and prepare a capon that "would only feed to music—one march in particular was its favorite." Earlier, this character sells a silver-chased belt for half a guilder while claiming it is worth two and sings "what fires that blood is my red meat" in a song used to peddle boots and food. This character's nickname recalls an incident in which she drove through gunfire in Riga to sell loaves of bread to soldiers, and in an attempt to warn her, her child dies while beating a drum. That girl, Kattrin, was this woman's last surviving child after the deaths of Eilif and Swiss Cheese. Name this title character of a Bertolt Brecht play.

The prelude of this work notes that the title figure is "condemned to strip himself stark naked" as the form of pathos, but is not allowed to "rush at you, roll you over, and squeeze your body for the briny drops." Character insights in this novel often come from Mrs. Mountstuard-Jenkinson, while its main action begins when Harry Oxford begins giving it to Constantia Durham, terminating her engagement to the title character. Vernon Whitford's education of Crossjay occupies much of the novel, and Clara Middleton contemplates marrying the protagonist, who is rejected by Laetitia Dale. Name this George Meredith novel about Sir Willoughby Patterne, the title narcissist.

This work's narrator recalls first seeing the main character's family being driven to church by a wild-eyed slave. One character tells his fifteen-year-old mistress, "Too bad you're not a mare like Penelope. Then I would give you a decent stall in the stable" because she had borne him a daughter, not a son. That man had cheated a Chickasaw chief out of a hundred acres of land and married Ellen as part of his "design" for greatness. Rosa helps explain why Henry killed Charles Bon rather than let him marry Judith to this book's narrator, Quentin Compson. Name this novel about Thomas Sutpen, one of many works set in Yoknapatawpha County by William Faulkner.

In this play, the lines "sleep rosebush" and "sleep carnation" follow mention of a lullaby, while one character drops orange blossoms a few days after hearing the neighing of another character's horse. Those two characters disappear together, leading all of the attendants at the title event to form a search party. The mother of a main character wishes her son had been born a girl so that he would not "find death by gun or knife". Act III features a discussion with three woodcutters and the entrance of both the Moon and Death. Eventually, that groom meets death disguised as a beggar woman before fighting Leonardo Felix to the death. Name this play depicting the title event, a work of Federico Garcia Lorca.

The speaker of this work judges "thy sword with its curve of lightning" more beautiful than "thy wristlet, decked with stars." Darius Milhaud set to music Andre Gide's French translation of this work. It mentions the "Kings of Kings" who presses "the signet of eternity." The speaker compares himself to a beggar maid and mentions a sea of light where butterflies spread their sails. One section of this collection begins "On the seashore of endless worlds children meet." Ending with the image of a "flock of homesick cranes", name this set of poems by Rabindranath Tagore.

One character created by a member of this family watches Verdi's Otello while fighting a need to go the bathroom; that character learns that Fat Vince is his father after being stalked by Frank the Phone and directing a film for Fielding Goodney. That member of this family, the creator of John Self, also wrote a novel about the Holocaust doctor Odilo Unverdorben that uses reverse chronology. Another member of this family wrote a novel about a man who mocks Professor Welch during a drunken speech on "Merrie England." give this surname shared by the author of Money and Time's Arrow and the author of Lucky Jim, Martin and his father Kingsley.

Several characters in this story sing the refrain "I'm proud to live in the service of the Lord, and I'm bound to die in his army" to the accompaniment of an accordion played by a character known as "The Innocent." The end of this story features an epitaph written on a deuce of clubs pinned to a pine tree, and in an earlier scene Uncle Billy runs off with all the mules. Its central character runs into Tom Simson and Piney Woods while on the way to Sandy Bar, but the entire party gets snowed in by a blizzard and perishes, including their leader, a gambler. Identify this story in which John Oakhurst leads the title group of exiles across the Sierras, a work by Bret Harte.

This man constantly recalls taking a seaside morning ride with his son before that son was killed in battle. This man's first love was Regina, a girl hanged by rebels. He was born on a mat, which presaged his humble beginnings as a friend of the mulatto Lunero, before shooting his own uncle caused this man to run away from home. This character is constantly brought back to consciousness by tapes of his dealings played back by Padilla. He married into the Bernal family for their lands and money after he betrayed the ideals of the Mexican Revolution. Name this character, businessman who recalls his life on his deathbed in a novel by Carlos Fuentes.
